element.def: A pure substance made of one kind of atom, defined by its number of protons. Carbon, oxygen and nitrogen are elements.

isotope.def: One of two or more forms of an element whose atoms have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Radioactive isotopes, such as phosphorus-32, can be traced through cells because they behave chemically like the ordinary atoms.

elements-of-life.def: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur (CHONPS), which together make up about 98% of the mass of living things.

matter-recycling.def: Atoms are not created or destroyed by living things: organisms take them in from the environment, rearrange them into new molecules and return them, so the same atoms cycle through air, water and organisms.

organic-molecule.def: A molecule built on a skeleton of carbon atoms, usually bonded to hydrogen. Water, carbon dioxide and salts are inorganic molecules.

carbon-skeleton.def: The chain, branched chain or ring of carbon atoms that forms the framework of an organic molecule. A molecule of only carbon and hydrogen is a hydrocarbon.

isomer.def: One of two or more molecules with the same chemical formula but different arrangements of atoms, and so different shapes and properties.

functional-group.def: A small cluster of atoms attached to a carbon skeleton that gives a molecule its chemical behavior, such as hydroxyl (–OH) or carboxyl (–COOH).

hydroxyl-group.def: –OH: a polar group that hydrogen-bonds with water and makes molecules such as sugars more soluble.

carboxyl-group.def: –COOH: an acidic group that releases a hydrogen ion and becomes –COO−. Every amino acid has one.

amino-group.def: –NH2: a basic group that picks up a hydrogen ion and becomes –NH3+. Every amino acid has one.

phosphate-group.def: A phosphorus atom bonded to four oxygens, carrying negative charge. Phosphate groups are part of nucleic acids, ATP and some lipids.

sulfhydryl-group.def: –SH: a sulfur-containing group. Two sulfhydryl groups can bond to each other, linking parts of a protein. It is found in the amino acid cysteine.

methyl-group.def: –CH3: a nonpolar group of one carbon and three hydrogens.

carbonyl-group.def: C=O: a carbon double-bonded to an oxygen; a polar group found in sugars.

carbohydrate.def: A sugar or a larger molecule built from sugars, made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Carbohydrates store energy and build structures.

lipid.def: A fat, oil or related molecule, made mostly of carbon and hydrogen, that does not dissolve in water because it is largely nonpolar.

amino-acid.def: The building block of proteins: a small molecule with an amino group and a carboxyl group. Every amino acid contains nitrogen; a few also contain sulfur.

protein.def: A large molecule made of one or more chains of amino acids; proteins do most of the work in cells.

nucleic-acid.def: A large molecule that stores or helps use the information in genes, such as DNA. Nucleic acids contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and phosphorus.

atp.def: Adenosine triphosphate: the molecule cells use to carry energy from where it is released to where it is used. It contains three phosphate groups.

photosynthesis-overview.def: The process by which plants, algae and some bacteria use the energy of light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.

respiration-overview.def: The process by which cells break down sugar, usually with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water and capturing the energy as ATP.

nitrogen-use.def: Organisms need nitrogen to build proteins (every amino acid contains it) and nucleic acids.

phosphorus-use.def: Organisms need phosphorus to build nucleic acids, ATP and some lipids, all of which contain phosphate groups.

sulfur-use.def: Organisms need sulfur because some amino acids, such as cysteine, contain it, so it is part of many proteins.
